pass_a_gloss: He will say in the ecclesiastical preaching that the word about the righteous anointing of God is contained, which, being believed to be true, also provokes to living well and fleeing from sin in every way, so that we may understand it, having taken the most necessary problem. And so that we may understand what the self-moved is, it is necessary to unfold the notion of it, so that with this having been clarified, what is being sought may be precisely presented. Of the things being moved, some have the cause of the movement in themselves, but others are moved only from outside. The things being carried, such as wood and stones and all matter being held together by habit alone, are moved only from outside. But let the word about the movement of bodies be left out for now, since there is no need for this for the present purpose. And animals and plants and all things that are held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved in themselves; from which they say metals are, and also fire is self-moved, and perhaps also springs. And of the things having the cause of being moved in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, but others from outside themselves; and the inanimate things are moved from outside themselves, but the animate things are moved from themselves. And the animate things are moved from themselves, a fantasy occurring and provoking an impulse. And again, in some of the animals, fantasies occur provoking an impulse, the natural fantasy moving the impulse in an orderly manner, as in the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the fantasy of its nature moving it in an orderly manner to this very thing, and no other thing is believed by the animal after its natural fantasy. And in the bee, to shape wax. But the rational animal also has reason in relation to its natural fantasy, approving and rejecting some fantasies, so that the animal may be led according to them. Whence, since in the nature of reason there are starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following which, having contemplated the good and the bad, we choose the good and turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy according to the opposite. It should not be ignored, however, that the greater part of the nature being ordered to all things is in the animals to a greater extent, or to a lesser extent, so that it is near, so to speak, to the work of reason in the tracking dogs and in the war horses. For the thing that is yielded to from outside, a fantasy moving us in such and such a way, is admittedly not in our power; but to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise is the work of our reason, either according to the starting points energizing us towards the impulses provoked to the good and duty, or turning us away to the opposite.

pass_b_english: He will say in the ecclesiastical preaching that the word about the righteous anointing of God is contained, and this word, being believed to be true, also provokes us to live well and to flee sin in every way. We must understand it, then, because we are confronting the most necessary problem. And so that we may understand what the self-moved is, it is necessary to unfold its notion, so that once this has been clarified, what is being sought may be precisely presented.

Of things that are moved, some have the cause of their movement in themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Things that are carried—such as wood, stones, and all matter held together by habit alone—are moved only from outside. Let the discussion of the movement of bodies be set aside for now, since it is not needed for the present purpose. Animals, plants, and in general all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved in themselves. From these, they say metals arise; in addition, fire is self-moved, and perhaps springs as well. Among the things that have the cause of being moved in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, but others from themselves in a different sense. The inanimate are moved from themselves in the first sense, while the animate are moved from themselves in the second. And animate things are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs and provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals, fantasies occur that provoke an impulse, their natural fantasy moving the impulse in an orderly manner. In the spider, a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, its natural fantasy moving it in an orderly manner to that very task, and the animal believes nothing else after its natural fantasy. In the bee, it is the impulse to shape wax.

But the rational animal also has reason alongside its natural fantasy, judging the fantasies—rejecting some and accepting others—so that it may be led according to them. Since the nature of reason contains starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following these we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad. We are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy when we do the opposite. It should not be ignored, however, that the greater part of the nature ordered toward all things exists in animals to a greater or lesser degree, so that it is near, so to speak, to the work of reason in tracking dogs and war horses. To yield to something from outside—a fantasy moving us this way or that—is admittedly not in our power. But to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise is the work of the reason within us, whether it energizes us according to the starting points toward the impulses provoked to the good and to duty, or turns us away to the opposite.

review.notes: Pass B fails to accurately translate the Greek regarding the inanimate and animate distinction in the second paragraph. The Greek states: 'τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα' (the inanimate [are moved] from themselves [sic - error in Greek/OCR or translation?], but the animate from themselves) and 'τὰ μέν φασιν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν χινεῖσϑαι, τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν' (some are said to be moved from themselves, others from themselves [sic]). However, looking at the specific text: 'τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα' (the inanimate, from themselves the animate) and 'τὰ μέν φασιν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν χινεῖσϑαι, τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν' (the former they say move from themselves, the latter from themselves). Pass B attempts to 'fix' the Greek by saying 'the inanimate are moved from themselves in the first sense, while the animate are moved from themselves in the second', which is a complete departure from the Greek text provided. More critically, the Greek 'τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα' is likely an OCR error for 'τὰ μὲν ἄψυχα ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν, τὰ δὲ ἔμψυχα ἐξ ἑαυτῶν' or similar, but as a reviewer, I must judge the provided text. Pass B's claim that 'the inanimate are moved from themselves' contradicts the Greek 'τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα' (which, even if garbled, does not support the 'first sense/second sense' distinction added by the translator). Furthermore, Pass B translates 'ἐπὶ τὸ χηροσπλαστεῖν' (to shape wax) as 'it is the impulse to shape wax', whereas the Greek is 'ἐπὶ τὸ χηροσπλαστεῖν' (to the [act of] wax-shaping/molding), which is acceptable, but the primary failure is the semantic invention in the movement section.
uncertainties: The Greek text contains significant OCR errors/corruptions (e.g., 'τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα' and 'τὰ μέν φασιν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν χινεῖσϑαι, τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν') which make a literal translation impossible, but Pass B introduces a 'first sense/second sense' distinction not present in the source.
reasons: Pass B adds information not present in the Greek: 'in the first sense... in the second sense' to explain the movement of inanimate/animate objects, which is an interpretive addition rather than a translation of the provided text 'τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα'.
